newsitem.title: GERMANY: DASA warns Bonn not to quit Eurofighter.
newsitem.headline: DASA warns Bonn not to quit Eurofighter.

text.p: The head of Daimler-Benz Aerospace (DASA), Manfred Bischoff, warned the German government on Tuesday there could be drastic consequences if it did not go ahead with a planned purchase of 180 Eurofighter jets.

His comments came amid speculation Bonn might withdraw from the project, jointly developed by Germany, Britain, Spain and Italy, under pressure to rein in the budget deficit this year to help Germany qualify for European monetary union (EMU).
"If Germany were not to go ahead with Eurofighter it would mean a dramatic weakening of the German aerospace industry," Bischoff of DASA, the German partner in the project, told Reuters.

Speaking through a DASA spokesman in Munich, he said a withdrawal would not only weaken German security, but would also have serious repercussions in terms of Germany's relations with the rest of Europe.
DASA's partners in the Eurofighter consortium are British Aerospace, Alenia Spa of Italy and state-owned CASA of Spain.
Bischoff argued that Germany risked losing technological know-how and many jobs for highly qualified workers.
A budget expert from the Free Democrats (FDP), coalition partners in Chancellor Helmut Kohl's coalition, said the German government could not afford to buy the Eurofighter plane.
"In the current budget situation it is completely impossible," Koppelin said on Tuesday.
Under pressure to tighten the budget deficit, Finance Minister Theo Waigel is expected to ask all government ministries for greater cost-cutting efforts.

Defence Minister Volker Ruehe, who wants Bonn to buy 180 Eurofighters for 23 billion marks ($13.5 billion), has said he can no longer rule out a German withdrawal from the project because of the budget problems.

Koppelin said before a final decision is taken on whether to order the planes, Bonn must consider whether production could be postponed, or whether industry could provide the upfront financing, the model used to produce submarines.
The decision whether to order the planes is expected to be taken by mid-summer, when Waigel draws up the budget for 1988.
Ruehe, in an interview published on Tuesday in the Westdeutsche Allgemeine Zeitung daily newspaper, said there was no further room for savings in the stretched defence budget.
Koppelin said DASA was wrong to argue that many jobs depend on the Eurofighter.

If Bonn goes ahead with a Eurofighter it cannot afford, that would jeopardise investments in other areas such as shipbuilding and tanks that also create jobs, he said. -- Fiona Fleck, Bonn Newsroom, 49-228-26097150
